title: Everyday Generative AI, From Awkward Emails to Dinner Plans
summary: Most chatbot use is advice, looking things up and writing. A tour of everyday AI uses at work and at home, the habit that improves them, and the rules to keep.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Ask a few friends what they actually do with ChatGPT or Claude and the answers are rarely dramatic. Fixing an email that sounds too blunt. Working out what a medication leaflet means. Planning a long weekend. Figuring out dinner from half a cabbage and three eggs.

The data says the same thing. A team of economists working with OpenAI studied ChatGPT conversations from its launch in November 2022 to July 2025. By then about 10% of the world's adults were using it, and three topics made up nearly 80% of conversations: practical guidance, seeking information and writing. Between June 2024 and June 2025, messages unrelated to work grew from 53% to more than 70% of all use (Chatterji et al., NBER, 2025). Anthropic's June 2026 report on Claude came at it from another angle and found a similar shape: the things people most often walked away with were explanations (17%), documents and reports (15%) and guidance (11%) (Anthropic Economic Index, June 2026).

So the everyday stuff is the main event. This post is a tour of it, sorted by part of life, so you can skip to yours and pick one thing to try this week. At the end you'll find the habit that makes every use on the list work better, plus a few ground rules.

What counts as generative AI here

Tools that make something new (text, images, audio, code) from a request written in plain language. As of November 2026 the best known are chat apps like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, plus the AI features built into mail, docs and phone keyboards. App names and features change every few months. The uses below hold up much longer.

One loop behind every use

Nearly every use in this post follows the same loop: say what you want, read the first draft, then react to it. "Shorter." "Less formal." "Keep option two, drop the rest." Three or four turns usually get you somewhere good.

A lot of the "AI is overrated" feeling comes from stopping after turn one. A model's first draft is like a first draft from a new teammate: worth reacting to, rarely ready to send. Once you treat it that way, the hundred separate "AI tricks" you see online collapse into one tool you point at different problems.

At work: writing and communication

At work, writing is where the use piles up. The NBER study found writing is the most common use at work, about 40% of work-related messages in June 2025. Anthropic's numbers lean the same way: documents and reports (20%) and email drafts (7%) are among the most common outputs of work conversations on Claude.

UseHow to do it
The awkward emailDescribe the situation and the tone ("polite but firm reminder about an overdue invoice") and ask for a draft you then edit.
Long threadsPaste a 40-message thread and ask what was decided, what is still open and who owns what.
Meeting notesTurn rough notes or a transcript into decisions, owners and dates. Check the owners against what people actually agreed to.
Tone fixes"Make this less defensive." "Say no without burning the bridge." "Cut it in half."
TranslationDraft in another language, then ask which phrases would sound odd to a native speaker. For anything that matters, have a native speaker read it.
Status updatesHand over five rough bullets and get back a weekly update with a clear structure.
Try this today

Take the email you've been putting off. Describe the situation in one sentence and ask for three versions: warm, neutral and firm. Pick the closest one and fix it by hand. The hard part was usually the opening line, and now you have one.

At work: thinking, planning and getting unstuck

The other big bucket in the data is guidance. At work, that looks like a thinking partner you can bother at 11 p.m. without feeling bad about it.

UseHow to do it
BrainstormingAsk for 20 options for a name, an angle or a feature, then keep three. The model brings volume. You do the picking.
Breaking down a project"50-person offsite in March, budget X: give me phases, tasks and a timeline." Then cross out what doesn't fit your team.
DecisionsLay out two options and ask which questions you haven't asked yet. That list is often more useful than a pros and cons table.
Arguing against yourself"What would a skeptical client push back on?" A free red team before the real meeting.
First drafts of docsJob descriptions, briefs, FAQs, proposals. A rough page beats a blank one.

At work: one use for your role

Every role has tasks that are mostly drafting, summarizing or reshaping text. Those are the easy wins. A starting map:

If you work in...Start with
Software engineeringExplaining unfamiliar code, writing tests for edge cases you list, drafting docs and migration notes. Read the diff the way you'd read a teammate's PR (more on that here).
MarketingVariants of one ad line, adapting one article for three channels, a dozen headline options to argue about.
SalesFirst drafts of outreach, call summaries, a list of likely objections before a meeting.
HR and recruitingJob descriptions, structured interview questions, policy drafts.
Data and analysisExplaining a formula, drafting SQL you then run and check yourself, putting results into plain language.
Support and operationsHelp-center drafts, turning repeated tickets into an FAQ, summarizing customer feedback.

Learning faster

Explanations are the most common thing people get from Claude in Anthropic's sample, and the share is even higher in personal chats, where a quarter of conversations produce one. A tutor who never sighs when you ask the same question twice turns out to be a popular idea.

UseHow to do it
Explain it at my level"Explain compound interest to a 12-year-old." Then: "Now explain it to someone who works in finance."
Start from what you know"I know basic Excel. Teach me pivot tables with a sales example."
Language practiceChat in the language you're learning and ask for corrections at the end, so the conversation keeps flowing.
Quiz yourselfPaste your notes, ask for ten questions, answer them, then ask what you got wrong and why.
The dense paragraphA contract clause, a medication leaflet, an RFC. Ask for plain words, then go back to the original for the parts that matter.
Study plans"I want to learn data analysis in 3 months with 5 hours a week. Give me a realistic plan."

Creative projects

Text is the default. As of November 2026, several of the big chat apps can also make images, and dedicated tools handle voice and short video. Quality varies a lot between tools and shifts with every update, so read the table as a list of what's possible.

MediumWhat you can do
WritingStories, speeches, lyrics, bios. Use it to get unstuck or to try three directions, then rewrite in your own voice.
ImagesConcept sketches, slide visuals and mockups from a text description.
Design helpColor palettes, layout ideas, copy that fits a mockup.
AudioDraft narration, text-to-speech for rehearsing a talk, podcast outlines.
VideoStoryboards, scripts, captions. Some tools generate short clips too, and results differ a lot from tool to tool.
Treat it like a collaborator

Good creative results take a few rounds: generate, react, refine. The model gives you a fast starting point. Your taste decides what's good.

Everyday life

This is where most of the growth has been. In the NBER data, non-work messages went from 53% to more than 70% of ChatGPT use. In Anthropic's sample, personal conversations rise from about 35% of the total on weekdays to just under 50% on weekends, and the most common things those personal chats produce are explanations (25%) and recommendations (22%).

AreaTry
CookingDinner from what's in the fridge, a week of meals, a swap for the ingredient you don't have.
TravelA day-by-day plan at your pace, a packing list, a rainy-day backup. Check opening hours and prices yourself, since they change.
MoneyExplain a term, sketch a budget, compare two savings options in plain words.
Shopping"Compare these two for someone who mostly cares about battery life." A list of questions to ask before you pay.
Words for the momentA wedding toast, a thank-you note, a hard message to a friend. Take the draft, then add your own memories.
Home and familyChore rotations, ideas for a rainy Sunday with kids, explaining a school topic.

Life admin and big decisions

Paperwork is boring and a little scary, which makes it a good fit for a patient explainer. Treat what you get back as a first pass from someone well read, and keep the final call yourself.

UseHow to do it
Read the fine printSummarize a lease or a terms-of-service page and list the clauses worth a closer look. Then read those clauses yourself.
Formal lettersA complaint, a request, a cover letter, a resignation note.
Compare optionsPhone plans, providers, products, measured against criteria you choose.
Rehearse a hard conversationA salary talk, a performance review, a tough call. Ask it to play the other side.
Prepare for a professionalGet oriented on a health, legal or tax question so you walk in with better questions.

The habit that makes all of this better

When one person gets a great answer and another gets mush from the same app, the difference is usually the request. Compare "give me a meal plan" with "meal plan for two adults, dinners under 30 minutes, one of us is vegetarian, we already have rice and eggs." The second one leaves the model far less to guess.

  • Say who it's for. "For a busy beginner" or "for a CFO with two minutes" changes the length, the vocabulary and the level of detail.
  • Give the background: what's going on, what you've tried, what matters to you. The model only knows what you tell it.
  • Set limits on length, format and what to skip. "Under 150 words, bullets, no jargon."
  • Iterate instead of restarting. "Good. More concrete, less formal."
Going deeper

Choosing what information to hand a model has a name: context engineering. It gets its own post in Context Engineering. To turn one-off chats into routines you repeat every week, see AI workflows that save hours.

A few ground rules

None of this works well without a few rules. They're short.

Check before you rely on it

Models can state wrong things with total confidence. A 2025 paper by researchers at OpenAI and Georgia Tech argues that's partly baked in: training and evaluation tend to reward guessing over admitting uncertainty (Kalai et al., 2025). For anything with real consequences (health, money, law, names, numbers, dates), treat the answer as a draft you still have to check.

  • Verify what matters. Confident and correct are different things. Check facts, figures and quotes before you act on them or pass them on. There's more on this in Reducing Hallucinations in LLMs.
  • Read the data settings. Consumer chat apps may keep what you type and learn from it, depending on your settings. Anthropic's consumer terms, for example, keep chats for five years if you allow training and 30 days if you don't, and business and API plans fall under separate terms (Anthropic, August 2025, checked November 2026). Other vendors have their own rules. Whatever the app, keep passwords, secrets and confidential company or customer data out of tools your organization hasn't approved.
  • Keep the decision with a person. AI drafts, you decide, and you own the result.
  • Use it to prepare for professionals. It's great for understanding a topic and asking sharper questions. Calls that need a doctor's, lawyer's or accountant's license still need that person.
  • Be open about it where it matters. Schools and workplaces set different rules. When in doubt, say you used it.

Try this week

  • Take the email you've been avoiding and ask for three versions in three tones.
  • Paste one long thread or document you need to read and ask what was decided and what's still open.
  • Ask for an explanation of something you usually nod along to, at your level, then one level deeper.
  • Before your next trip or big purchase, ask for a comparison against criteria you write yourself.
  • Open the data settings in the chat app you use and see what it keeps.

Want the bigger picture, from writing prompts to working with agents? AI Literacy is the next read.

faqs.q: What do people actually use generative AI for?
faqs.a: Mostly everyday help. A study of ChatGPT conversations from November 2022 to July 2025 found that practical guidance, seeking information and writing made up nearly 80% of conversations, and more than 70% of messages weren't about work. Anthropic's June 2026 report on Claude lists explanations, documents and reports, and guidance as the most common outputs.

faqs.q: How do I get better answers from AI tools?
faqs.a: Give more context. Say who the answer is for, describe your situation and what you've already tried, set limits on length and format, then react to the first draft instead of starting over. Weak answers usually come from requests that leave the model guessing.

faqs.q: Do AI chat apps keep or train on what I type?
faqs.a: It depends on the app, the plan and your settings. Anthropic's consumer terms from August 2025, for example, keep chats for five years if you allow training and 30 days if you don't, while business and API plans have separate terms. Check your app's data settings, and keep passwords and confidential data out of tools your organization hasn't approved.

faqs.q: Can generative AI do more than text?
faqs.a: Yes. As of November 2026, several chat apps can also create images, and dedicated tools generate voice and short video. Quality varies a lot between tools. For creative work, expect a few rounds of generating and refining before you get something you like.

faqs.q: Can I rely on AI for health, legal or money questions?
faqs.a: Use it to understand the topic and prepare better questions, then confirm with a professional. Models can state wrong things confidently, partly because training and evaluation tend to reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, so anything with real consequences needs checking.
